newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Riksbank says Sweden can meet EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: Riksbank says Sweden can meet EMU criteria.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Wednesday Sweden had a good chance of meeting the European Union's convergence criteria for EMU participation from its 1999 start.

Central bank governor Urban Backstrom said in a speech in Brussels -- a copy of which was made available to Reuters in Stockholm -- that he had noted a disturbing tendency with respect to how countries not using the euro currency are treated within the EU's TARGET system.

TARGET is the future European network which will link interbank money markets across Europe to the future European Central Bank and join national computer systems for large-value payments in the euro.
"There is a desire among some countries to postpone the decision about this until the ECB has been established and to provide full access to the system only to EMU countries," Backstrom said.

"That would mean only those countries which participate in EMU from the start will be able to influence this matter and that financial institutions will be hit by negative competitive conditions because some countries do not belong to EMU initially.

Some German and French bankers have been campaigning to exclude banks in non-EMU countries from full access to TARGET on the grounds this could potentially affect money supply within the single currency.
Backstrom said this was an example of a disturbing tendency in the relationship between "ins" and "outs".
"What is at stake is potential conflicts between the EU's member states and their respective financial systems, entirely contrary to the overriding purpose of the European process," he said.
He said there were dangers in building irrelevant barriers and restrictions for the financial sector in Europe.
"There are reasons to believe that we will not be shifting activity from one European country to another but could instead be shifting activity away from Europe altogether," Backstrom said.
Backstrom said Sweden was still debating whether it will join the first group of countries that establish EMU in Janaury 1999 or whether it would postpone joining.

But he said substantial improvements have happened in Sweden even though unemployment was still high, government debt was still relatively high at just under 80 percent of Gross Domestic Product, and wage formation had not yet fully adapted to an economy with low inflation.
"It is my assessment that Sweden stands a good change of meeting the convergence criteria for participation in the EMU right from the start," he said.
